lessons.title: Transformations, reductions and lazy iteration
lessons.summary: Read closure-based collection pipelines from first principles and distinguish output shape, dropped values and deferred work.
objectives: Explain a closure parameter before using map, filter, compactMap or flatMap.
Choose the output shape and failure policy of a transformation.
Predict reduction order and distinguish lazy description from cached results.

sections.title: Make the collection rule readable before making it short
sections.html:
On Android you may chain map, filter and a Sequence to prepare list content. Swift has analogous standard-library operations, but the result shape, optional policy and evaluation timing deserve explicit reasoning. Begin with a for loop in your head: which inputs are visited, which outputs are appended, and what happens when an input is invalid? A pipeline is a compact expression of that algorithm. It should not replace that explanation. These operations are synchronous unless a different API explicitly states asynchronous effects; a function named map does not imply concurrency.

A closure is an unnamed function value that can be passed to another operation. Its inputs and result follow a function type, such as (Int) -> Int. Braces surround its definition, in separates parameter declarations from the body, and the body may return a value. We introduce just the closure syntax needed to transform local values here. Storage, escaping and ownership are taught separately in lesson 068. The standard eager Array operations produce new arrays. Kotlin collection operations provide a useful algorithm analogy, but do not assume Swift’s generic Sequence means a lazy Kotlin Sequence.

sections.title: A small complete pipeline explained from its inputs
sections.html:
let values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
let double: (Int) -> Int = { value in
    return value * 2
}
let doubled = values.map(double)
let even = values.filter { value in
    return value % 2 == 0
}
print(doubled)
print(even)

Line one is the input array. The next declaration gives double an explicit function type: one Int enters, one Int returns. The closure’s local parameter is value, and return computes twice that value. Passing double to map supplies the operation to apply for each element; it does not call double once and pass one result. Map keeps one output per input and order, so doubled is [2, 4, 6, 8]. The filter call uses trailing-closure syntax: the closure appears after the function name instead of as a labeled argument inside parentheses.

Filter’s closure returns Bool and decides whether the original element is retained. It does not replace that element with true or false. Even is [2, 4]. With a single expression, a closure can omit return; Swift can infer its parameter/result types from the surrounding operation. Shorthand $0 means the first implicit closure parameter and $1 the second. Use explicit names until you can read the full rule. Kotlin often uses it for a single lambda parameter; Swift does not. A trailing closure is ordinary function-value syntax, not a special concurrent block. Map preserves multiplicity unless your transform itself changes the values.

sections.title: Compact and flatten are two different shape decisions
sections.html:
let texts = ["3", "bad", "8"]
let attempts: [Int?] = texts.map { text in Int(text) }
let valid: [Int] = texts.compactMap { text in Int(text) }
let groups = [[1, 2], [], [3]]
let flattened = groups.flatMap { group in group }
print(attempts.count)
print(valid)
print(flattened)

Int(text) is a failable initializer returning Int? because not every String spells an integer. Map retains one optional output per input, so attempts has three entries, including nil for bad. CompactMap accepts a transform returning an optional and drops nil outputs, producing [3, 8]. This drop is a policy: invalid rows disappear. It can be suitable for optional decoration and unsuitable for a form where the user needs an error for each invalid entry. Keep the original text or a result record when rejection must remain visible.

FlatMap in this example accepts a transform producing a sequence for each input group, then concatenates the elements into one array. The result is [1, 2, 3]. It flattens one nesting layer; it does not recursively flatten arbitrary data or automatically skip domain errors. Historical Swift code sometimes used flatMap for optional removal; modern explicit compactMap makes today’s intention clearer. Kotlin mapNotNull resembles compactMap’s shape, and flatMap has a related flattening role, but neither analogy chooses your error policy. Map with an optional-returning transform is not a compile error: [Int?] may be exactly what the consumer needs.

sections.title: Reduce a sequence into one explicit accumulator
sections.html:
let values = [1, 2, 3]
let sum = values.reduce(0) { total, value in
    return total + value
}
let labels = ["a", "b", "a"]
let counts = labels.reduce(into: [String: Int]()) { counts, label in
    counts[label, default: 0] += 1
}
print(sum)
print(counts["a"] ?? -1)
print([Int]().reduce(10) { total, value in total + value })

Reduce starts from its initial value, here zero. At each step its closure receives the accumulated total and the next input, returning the next total. The progression is zero, one, three, six. An empty input returns the initial value, so the final expression produces ten. Order matters for noncommutative operations such as concatenation or subtraction. A reduction does not guarantee the chosen integer arithmetic cannot overflow; input bounds remain part of the contract.

Reduce(into:) passes a mutable accumulator to its closure and expects mutation rather than a returned replacement. The typed empty dictionary establishes [String: Int], and the familiar default subscript increments a count. This can avoid repeatedly constructing new collection values for an accumulating collection. It is still a synchronous operation and does not synchronize concurrent access. Kotlin fold provides a useful accumulation analogy, but Swift’s into form has a mutation contract that we will connect to inout in lesson 064. Choose it from the output and mutation requirements, not from an unmeasured performance claim. A clearer for loop remains a good option when error handling or intermediate evidence matters.

sections.title: Deferred work is not remembered work
sections.html:
let values = [1, 2, 3, 4]
var visits = 0
let pipeline = values.lazy.map { value in
    visits += 1
    return value * 10
}
print(visits)
let firstTwo = Array(pipeline.prefix(2))
print(firstTwo)
print(visits)
let firstTwoAgain = Array(pipeline.prefix(2))
print(firstTwoAgain)
print(visits)

Lazy creates an adapter that describes how to obtain elements when a consumer requests them. Defining this pipeline does not invoke the map transform, so the first print is zero. Materializing its first two mapped values with Array produces [10, 20], with two visits in this simple lazy-map example. Asking again obtains those values again and the final visit count is four. The adapter does not memoize the transformed results. If the consumer needs a stable result snapshot, store the materialized array rather than repeatedly traversing a side-effectful pipeline.

The counter exists only to make evaluation visible. Real transforms should usually be pure, because lazy traversal can repeat evaluation and different adapters/collection operations may visit elements differently. Do not generalize this precise count to every lazy-filter pipeline. A Sequence only promises iteration; some sequences are single-pass and cannot be safely replayed. Arrays are repeatable collections. Sorting needs the relevant values and produces an eager ordered result; a lazy prefix cannot make an arbitrary global sort inspect just two inputs. Kotlin Sequence is a helpful deferred-evaluation analogy, while Swift Sequence is the broader iteration protocol and lazy is an explicit adapter.

sections.title: Read actual transformations through their shape
sections.html:
The active Sequence.flatSorted helper compactMaps optional sort keys into tuples, sorts those tuples, then maps back to original elements. You can now identify where rows without keys disappear and how the output shape changes. Key-path access is separate syntax for later study; today read the transform’s return shape. In the cancellation controller’s selectedOption helper, filter keeps selected options before soleItem asks whether exactly one remains. That differs from simply choosing the first selected item. Its count/absence rule matters to domain correctness.

Misconceptions include expecting filter to produce Bools, assuming compactMap reports parse failures, expecting a lazy adapter to cache, and treating all Sequence operations as lazy. Rewrite a suspect chain as a loop and label each intermediate type. A valid pipeline can still lose required data: converting bad input to nil and dropping it may hide a validation error. If ordering matters, check where a sort or set conversion enters the chain. We verified these repository helpers and their source membership, but did not benchmark them or establish asynchronous behavior. The standalone exercise measures only its specified local outputs and evaluation counts.

quiz.question: What shape does map { Int($0) } produce for String inputs?
options: A thrown error for every invalid String
quiz.explanation: Int(String) is failable, and map retains each optional result. compactMap is the operation that deliberately drops nil outputs.

quiz.question: Does .lazy cache transformed elements?
options: No; later traversal can evaluate them again
quiz.explanation: Lazy defers production. Materializing an Array stores a result snapshot; the adapter itself does not promise memoization.

quiz.question: What is reduce’s result for an empty input?
quiz.explanation: There are no steps to apply, so the provided initial value is returned. The type and value need not be an integer or zero.

exercise.brief: Parse synthetic quantity strings while retaining invalid-input evidence, then compare eager and lazy output production.
steps: Use [2, bad, 5] and create mapped optionals plus compacted integers.
State why counting valid values alone would hide a rejected input.
Sum valid integers with reduce and test an empty-input total.
Construct a lazy doubled array prefix with an invocation counter.
Traverse twice and explain why production repeats without claiming a general performance result.
acceptance: The mapped result has three positions and the compacted result is [2, 5].
The valid sum is seven and an empty sum with initial zero is zero.
A lazy adapter performs no mapping until consumed.
The answer explicitly reports one invalid input instead of treating dropped data as full success.
exercise.solution:
This complete standalone program makes each output shape explicit. The discarded-input count is a small diagnostic for these fixtures, not a full parser error model.

let texts = ["2", "bad", "5"]
let attempts = texts.map { text in Int(text) }
let valid = texts.compactMap { text in Int(text) }
print(attempts.count)
print(valid)
print(attempts.count - valid.count)
print(valid.reduce(0) { total, value in total + value })
print([Int]().reduce(0) { total, value in total + value })
var calls = 0
let doubled = valid.lazy.map { value in
    calls += 1
    return value * 2
}
print(calls)
print(Array(doubled.prefix(1)))
print(Array(doubled.prefix(1)))
print(calls)

The output is three, [2, 5], one, seven, zero, zero, [4], [4], two. Both materializations request the first mapped value again. Map retained the rejected position, while compactMap removed it. A user-facing parser should usually preserve which original text failed and the reason, rather than only a count; lesson 067 introduces enum/error representations for that purpose.

For retrieval, change bad to a valid three and predict the new count and sum before running. Then explain whether your product should reject an entire batch or accept valid entries with explicit rejection evidence. The language operations permit either policy; they do not choose it. A passing synthetic pipeline does not verify real networking, asynchronous cancellation, performance or learner mastery.
